Name: mechanistic_degeneracy_probing
Title: Many Roads, One Outcome: Do Scientific Foundation Models Represent Distinct Mechanistic Routes to the Same Observable?
Short Hypothesis: In many scientific systems, the same observable outcome can arise from distinct underlying mechanisms (mechanistic degeneracy): a protein can be destabilized by breaking a disulfide, disrupting a salt bridge, or exposing the hydrophobic core; a reaction can be slowed by a leaving-group effect, a steric effect, or a solvent effect; a material's low conductivity can stem from a bandgap or from disorder. A model that merely predicts the outcome (a scalar) may collapse these routes into one indistinct representation, whereas a model with mechanistic understanding should internally separate them into distinct route-specific directions even when the final scalar output is identical. We hypothesize that current scientific foundation models partially preserve this mechanistic degeneracy internally, that the degree of route separability is a read-only diagnostic distinguishing mechanistic understanding from outcome-fitting, and that route-separability predicts a model's ability to generalize interventions across routes.
Related Work: Prior interpretability of scientific foundation models tests whether a single concept/mechanism is present (BERTology-Meets-Biology, SAE protein features), whether laws are causally used, whether scaling exponents or conservation laws are encoded, or whether relational ontologies are recovered. Mechanistic simulation work (Macklin et al. 2020, Science) cross-validates heterogeneous data through a single explicit mechanistic model but does not probe learned representations. Crucially, none of this work asks whether a model internally distinguishes *multiple different mechanisms that produce the same observable outcome* (mechanistic degeneracy / many-to-one maps). This is a distinct and unexplored question: standard probing measures whether the outcome or one mechanism is encoded, but a model can perfectly predict a scalar outcome while being blind to which of several routes produced it. Our contribution is a read-only framework that measures route separability among outcome-matched inputs, distinguishing 'knows the answer' from 'knows why', and links route separability to cross-route intervention generalization. This differs from all prior work and from my previous proposals (which target laws, exponents, universality, superseded theories, conservation, ontology geometry, validity domains, and causal asymmetry).
Abstract: A deep feature of scientific systems is mechanistic degeneracy: the same measurable outcome can be produced by qualitatively different mechanisms. A protein's melting temperature can be lowered by breaking a disulfide bond, disrupting a salt bridge, or exposing its hydrophobic core; a reaction rate can be reduced by steric, electronic, or solvent effects; a material can be an insulator due to a wide bandgap or to disorder. A model that only fits the scalar outcome need not know which route produced it, whereas a model that understands the domain should internally separate these routes even when outcomes coincide. We introduce Mechanistic-Degeneracy Probing, a read-only framework that tests whether foundation models preserve route identity among outcome-matched inputs. For each of ~10 outcomes with multiple known causal routes across biology, chemistry, and materials, we assemble sets of inputs that produce nearly identical outcomes via different mechanisms, then measure (i) whether representations cluster/separate by route (a linear route classifier's accuracy at matched output), (ii) whether route directions are geometrically distinct and stable across layers, and (iii) whether route separability predicts cross-route intervention generalization: a route-specific edit learned on one mechanism should transfer to inputs using the same route but not across routes. We define a Route-Separability Score and benchmark it against randomly-initialized and outcome-shuffled controls. Applied to open protein (ESM-2), molecular (ChemBERTa/MolFormer), and materials models, the framework yields a cheap, reproducible audit of whether scientific models know not just the answer but which mechanism produced it.
Experiments: 1. Outcome-and-route curation (~10 outcomes, each with >=2 distinct mechanistic routes and a way to match outcomes): proteins -- lowered melting temperature via (a) disulfide loss, (b) salt-bridge disruption, (c) hydrophobic-core exposure, using MegaScale/FireProtDB ddG deep mutational scans binned so that different mechanistic mutation classes yield matched ddG; loss of function via active-site vs. fold-destabilizing mutations. Chemistry -- reduced reaction rate via steric vs. electronic vs. solvent effects (public reaction/kinetics datasets with substituent annotations, Hammett/steric parameters); low solubility via lipophilicity vs. crystal-packing routes. Materials -- low electrical conductivity / insulating behavior via wide-bandgap vs. disorder routes (Materials Project + annotated structure types). Each outcome provides route labels and outcome values for matching. 2. Outcome matching: within each outcome, select input subsets so route groups have statistically indistinguishable outcome distributions (matched means/variances via propensity-style matching), so any representational separation cannot be explained by output differences. 3. Models: ESM-2 (8M-650M) for protein routes, ChemBERTa/MolFormer for chemistry routes, a public materials/crystal encoder for materials routes; extract token/pooled representations at all layers. 4. Route separability: fit a linear (and nonlinear robustness-check) route classifier on representations restricted to outcome-matched inputs; report per-layer route-classification accuracy/AUROC. Because outcomes are matched, above-chance route accuracy indicates the model encodes mechanism beyond outcome. 5. Route geometry: extract per-route mean directions, measure inter-route angular separation (cosine/CKA) and within-route compactness (silhouette), and track stability across layers. 6. Route-Separability Score (RSS): aggregate matched-outcome route AUROC, inter-route separation, and layer stability, per outcome. 7. Controls: (a) outcome-shuffled null (shuffle route labels), (b) randomly-initialized-model control, (c) an outcome-only baseline showing that a probe trained to predict the scalar outcome does NOT recover route (route separation is orthogonal to outcome), and (d) a surface-feature baseline (can route be trivially read from input tokens? report how much RSS exceeds this). 8. Cross-route intervention-generalization validation: learn a route-specific activation edit (steering direction) that shifts the outcome using route A inputs; test whether applying it transfers correctly to held-out route-A inputs but fails/behaves differently on route-B inputs producing the same outcome. Correlate per-outcome RSS with the specificity of this transfer (transfer-within-route minus transfer-across-route). 9. Scaling analysis: track RSS across model sizes to test whether mechanistic-route resolution emerges with scale. Metrics: matched-outcome route AUROC, inter-route separation, RSS, RSS-vs-transfer-specificity correlation, and RSS margin over surface-feature baseline. Deliverable: an open outcome-with-multiple-routes benchmark and per-model Route-Separability leaderboard across public scientific models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Route separation could reflect surface-feature differences (e.g., disulfide mutations look lexically different from salt-bridge mutations) rather than mechanism understanding; the surface-feature baseline is central and RSS is reported as a margin over it, and we prefer routes whose surface features are as similar as possible. 2. Perfect outcome matching is hard; residual outcome differences could leak into route classification, so we report route accuracy as a function of matching tightness and include the outcome-only probe control. 3. Curating outcomes with cleanly labeled multiple routes is easiest in proteins (mutation-class annotations) and chemistry (mechanistic parameters) and harder in materials; some materials outcomes may support only binary route tests. 4. Routes may be encoded nonlinearly; we add nonlinear-probe robustness checks and treat linear separability as a lower bound. 5. The intervention-transfer validation relies on activation steering, which can go off-manifold; we cross-check with patching from real inputs and report transfer specificity as validation evidence, not proof. 6. Above-chance route separation does not by itself prove correct mechanistic causal use; the transfer-specificity link is designed to make separation actionable, and negative/partial results are themselves informative diagnostics. 7. Findings are outcome- and model-specific, but this diagnostic specificity is the intended output.
